name: Degenerative meniscal tear
summary: A slowly developing meniscal lesion, usually a horizontal cleavage of the medial posterior horn in people over 35, often an early feature of osteoarthritis. Exercise therapy is first-line, not arthroscopy.

keyFacts.label: First-line care
keyFacts.value: Supervised exercise therapy and education for about 12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Arthroscopy
keyFacts.value: Partial meniscectomy is no better than sham surgery or exercise; not first-line

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs if needed; MRI is usually not indicated first-line

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Present on MRI in 19–56% of people aged 50–90; most are asymptomatic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Over 35 years; most common from 50 onwards

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over 3–6 months, continuing to 2 years

overview:
A degenerative meniscal lesion develops slowly, without significant trauma, in a person older than 35 years; it typically involves a horizontal cleavage of the medial posterior horn [r1]. Meniscal tears are a common incidental finding on MRI in middle-aged and older adults and frequently do not cause symptoms [r2]. In this age group meniscal damage is better viewed as a feature of early knee osteoarthritis than as an isolated injury [r3].

High-quality trials have changed practice. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy (APM) was no better than sham surgery, including for patients with catching or locking [r4,r5], and was not superior to supervised exercise therapy [r6,r7]. The ESSKA consensus states that APM should not be offered as first-line treatment [r1], and a BMJ Rapid Recommendation advises against arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease [r8]. The physiotherapist therefore leads first-line care: education, progressive exercise therapy and load management.

epidemiology.text: In a population-based MRI study of 991 adults aged 50–90 years, the prevalence of a meniscal tear or destruction ranged from 19% in women aged 50–59 to 56% in men aged 70–90, and 61% of people with a tear had no knee pain, aching or stiffness in the previous month [r2]. Among people with radiographic osteoarthritis, tears were equally common with and without symptoms (63% vs 60%) [r2]. A meta-analysis found strong evidence that age over 60, male sex, work-related kneeling and squatting, and climbing more than 30 flights of stairs a day are risk factors for degenerative tears [r9].

intrinsic: Radiographic knee osteoarthritis and cartilage loss [r2,r3]
Higher body mass and varus alignment, which concentrate load on the medial compartment (body mass is modifiable)
extrinsic: Climbing more than 30 flights of stairs a day [r9]
Repeated deep loaded flexion (e.g. gardening, tiling, plumbing)

mechanism.summary: There is no significant injury. With age and cumulative compressive load, the meniscal matrix loses its organisation and strength, so a trivial movement such as rising from a squat with a small twist is enough to complete a tear. Shear stress within the wedge produces a horizontal cleavage, most often in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, where compressive load in flexion is greatest [r1,r10].
sequence: Years of compressive load, especially in deep flexion, act on a meniscus whose matrix is ageing.
Proteoglycan and water content change, collagen bundles become disorganised and cells decline, reducing the tissue's capacity.
Shear stress between the femoral and tibial surfaces of the wedge starts an intrasubstance horizontal split in the posterior horn.
An everyday movement (rising from a squat, kneeling or turning) completes the cleavage, sometimes with a felt twinge.
Pain develops gradually at the medial joint line, often with intermittent swelling from synovitis.
The meniscus may extrude from the joint margin and lose its load-sharing function, increasing cartilage stress and progressing osteoarthritis [r3].

variants.name: Posterior medial root tear
variants.description: A low-energy radial tear at the posterior root (often a 'pop' while squatting) abolishes hoop function, causes extrusion and accelerates medial compartment degeneration.

variants.name: Asymptomatic incidental tear
variants.description: Most degenerative tears found on MRI cause no symptoms; the patient's pain may come from osteoarthritis, synovitis or another source [r2].

variants.name: Parameniscal cyst
variants.description: Synovial fluid tracks through a horizontal cleavage to form a cyst at the joint line, more often laterally.

anatomy.text: The menisci are wedge-shaped fibrocartilages whose circumferential type I collagen bundles convert compressive load into hoop stress, sharing load across the tibiofemoral joint and protecting the articular cartilage [r10]. Only the peripheral 10–25% is vascularised, so the inner tissue relies on diffusion from synovial fluid. With ageing the matrix changes in composition and cellularity, which reduces its mechanical properties [r10]. The medial meniscus is anchored to the capsule and deep MCL and its posterior horn carries most load in flexion, which explains why degenerative tears cluster there. The anterior and posterior horns and the peripheral rim are innervated; the inner tissue is not.

structures.name: Medial meniscus posterior horn
structures.role: Main load-bearing segment in flexion; commonest site of degenerative tears

structures.name: Meniscal roots
structures.role: Anchor the horns so hoop stress can develop; root failure functionally removes the meniscus

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.role: Shares load with the meniscus; degenerates alongside it in osteoarthritis [r3]

structures.name: Synovium and capsule
structures.role: Richly innervated; synovitis and effusion are major pain sources in degenerative knees

structures.name: Quadriceps
structures.role: Primary shock absorber and target of exercise therapy

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Degenerative meniscal lesions reflect a mismatch between cumulative load and declining tissue capacity rather than a single overload. The ageing matrix loses its organised collagen network, develops mucoid change and fissures, and becomes less able to resist shear. Horizontal cleavages begin within the substance of the wedge and extend to a free edge; flap, complex and radial components may follow [r1,r10].

Meniscal damage, cartilage loss, bone marrow lesions and synovitis frequently coexist. Damaged menisci tend to extrude and transmit less load, so meniscal pathology is both a consequence and a driver of osteoarthritis: the risk of osteoarthritis rises sharply once the meniscus is damaged [r3]. Because tears are so common in asymptomatic knees, a tear seen on MRI is not necessarily the cause of a patient's pain [r2].

structures.name: Medial meniscus
structures.effect: Horizontal cleavage, fraying and maceration of the posterior horn; may extrude beyond the tibial margin

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Coexisting thinning and fibrillation in the same compartment (early osteoarthritis) [r3]

structures.name: Subchondral bone
structures.effect: Bone marrow lesions under overloaded cartilage contribute to pain

structures.name: Synovium
structures.effect: Effusion-synovitis is common; in a trial cohort with meniscal tear and osteoarthritis, 52% had medium or large effusion-synovitis on MRI [r11]

structures.name: Meniscal roots
structures.effect: Posterior root tears cause extrusion and rapid compartment overload

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Weakness and arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion and pain; strength deficits improve with exercise therapy [r6,r12]

muscles.name: Hip abductors
muscles.effect: Weakness increases knee adduction moment and medial compartment load

muscles.name: Hamstrings and calf
muscles.effect: Guarding and reduced use; contribute to stiffness and altered gait

cellular.description: Fewer and less active meniscal cells, altered proteoglycan and water content, and disorganised collagen reduce tensile and shear strength [r10].
Mucoid degeneration and microfissures develop within the wedge, seen on MRI as increased signal before a surface tear appears.
Once the cleavage reaches a surface, debris and cytokines provoke synovitis and effusion, which drive pain flares.
Degenerative tears are largely in poorly vascular, low-cellularity tissue and do not heal; symptoms improve through settling of synovitis and better muscle function rather than tissue repair.

systems.effect: Pain arises from synovium, capsule, subchondral bone and innervated meniscal horns. Central sensitisation and pain beliefs influence symptom severity, so MRI findings correlate poorly with pain [r2].
Synovitis is common and fluctuates, explaining intermittent swelling and pain flares [r11].
Reduced knee flexion and extension moments, weaker hip abductors and avoidance of stairs and squatting further decondition the limb.
Being told the knee has a 'tear' encourages fear of movement and expectation of surgery; reassurance and explanation of normal age-related findings are therapeutic.
Meniscal damage is a marker and driver of incipient osteoarthritis; removing meniscal tissue may add to that risk [r3].

grading.system: MRI meniscal signal grade (intrasubstance to surface tear)

grades.description: Globular increased signal within the meniscus not reaching an articular surface (intrasubstance degeneration).
grades.prognosis: Common with ageing; not a tear

grades.description: Linear increased signal within the meniscus not reaching a surface.
Increased signal reaching an articular surface: a tear (horizontal, flap, radial or complex).
grades.prognosis: Frequently asymptomatic in older adults; manage according to symptoms, not the image [r2]

grades.description: Posterior root disruption with meniscal extrusion beyond the tibial margin.
grades.prognosis: Associated with faster medial compartment degeneration

timeframes.summary: There is no tissue-healing timeline: improvement comes from settling synovitis, restoring muscle function and managing load. Expect gradual improvement over 3–6 months with exercise therapy, continuing to 2 years.

healing.description: Pain and effusion settle with load modification and early exercise
Early gains in function and confidence; quadriceps activation improves
Muscle hypertrophy and improved load tolerance; outcomes continue to improve to 2 years [r6,r7]

milestones.label: Pain-guided return to walking and daily activity
Strength superior to APM group
milestones.note: Thigh strength improved more with exercise than surgery at 3 months [r6]

milestones.label: Review of exercise response
milestones.note: ESSKA uses about 3 months of non-operative care as the threshold before considering APM [r13]

milestones.label: Outcomes equal to surgery
milestones.note: No clinically relevant difference vs APM at 2 years [r6,r7]

timeframes.returnToSport: Most people return to walking, recreational sport and work within weeks, guided by symptoms. Higher-impact or deep-flexion activities return gradually over 3–6 months as strength and effusion allow.

symptoms: Gradual onset of medial (less often lateral) knee pain without significant trauma, sometimes after a minor twist or rising from a squat
Pain with squatting, kneeling, stairs and turning
Intermittent swelling and stiffness, especially after activity
Catching or clicking sensations (these are common and do not predict benefit from surgery) [r5]
Night pain or pain at rest during flares
signs: Pain at end-range flexion; extension usually preserved
Quadriceps weakness and reduced single-leg control
Features of osteoarthritis such as crepitus, bony enlargement or varus alignment

subjective: Onset: no or trivial trauma, age over 35, gradual symptoms
Distinguish true locking (cannot extend, needs manoeuvring) from catching or a feeling of instability
Pain pattern: activity-related versus rest and night pain (flare, bone marrow lesion, insufficiency fracture)
Occupational and leisure exposure to kneeling, squatting and stairs
Expectations and beliefs about the 'tear' and surgery; previous MRI reports
General health, body mass, other joint pain and red flags
observation: Varus or valgus alignment and gait (lateral thrust)
Bony enlargement of the joint margins (osteoarthritis)
palpation: Effusion grading with the stroke test
rangeOfMotion: Flexion often painful and limited at end range
Extension usually full; a springy block suggests a displaced fragment
Hip range of motion to exclude referred hip pain
strength: Quadriceps strength and activation (lag on straight-leg raise)

specialTests.name: Joint-line tenderness
specialTests.purpose: Localise medial or lateral compartment pain
specialTests.procedure: With the knee flexed to about 90°, palpate the joint line from anterior to posterior and compare with the other knee.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain at the joint line. Specificity is likely to be lower when osteoarthritis coexists.

specialTests.name: McMurray test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain or a click from the posterior horn
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Fully flex the knee, rotate the tibia and extend with a varus or valgus stress while palpating the joint line.
specialTests.positive: Painful click at the joint line.

specialTests.name: Thessaly test (20°)
specialTests.procedure: Patient stands on the affected leg, knee flexed 20°, holding the examiner's hands, and rotates three times each way. Use caution in older adults with poor balance.

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome (KOOS4) in exercise vs surgery trials [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: WOMET (Western Ontario Meniscal Evaluation Tool)
outcomeMeasures.use: Meniscus-specific quality of life; primary outcome in the sham-surgery trial [r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: IKDC Subjective Knee Form
outcomeMeasures.use: Knee function; primary outcome in the ESCAPE trial [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: 30 s chair stand and 40 m fast-paced walk
outcomeMeasures.use: Performance-based function in middle-aged and older adults

imaging.indication: Recommended imaging when imaging is needed: to identify osteoarthritis, alignment, or rare pathology such as tumour or fracture [r1]
imaging.findings: Joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, alignment; often normal early

imaging.indication: Not indicated in the first-line work-up [r1]. Consider for persistent symptoms after non-operative care, suspected insufficiency fracture, true locking or atypical features.
imaging.findings: Horizontal or complex tear of the medial posterior horn, extrusion, root tear, cartilage loss, bone marrow lesions, effusion-synovitis

differentials.name: Knee osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Often coexists. Age over 45, activity-related pain, short morning stiffness, crepitus and radiographic change; management overlaps.

differentials.name: Traumatic meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Younger patient with a clear twisting injury, delayed effusion and mechanical symptoms; repair may be appropriate.

differentials.name: Pes anserine tendinopathy / bursitis
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness 2–5 cm below the medial joint line over the pes insertion rather than at the joint line.

differentials.name: Subchondral insufficiency fracture (SIFK)
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden severe medial pain without trauma in an older adult, often with night pain and inability to weight-bear; bone marrow oedema on MRI.

differentials.name: Articular cartilage defect
differentials.distinguishing: Activity-related effusion and pain from a focal chondral lesion; MRI distinguishes.

differentials.name: Referred hip pain
differentials.distinguishing: Reduced, painful hip internal rotation reproduces thigh or knee pain; knee examination is unremarkable.

redFlags: True locked knee (a mechanical block to extension): arrange orthopaedic review; this is uncommon in degenerative tears.

Sudden severe knee pain without trauma, night pain or inability to weight-bear in an older adult: suspect subchondral insufficiency fracture or osteonecrosis. Arrange MRI and medical review; protect weight-bearing.
Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or systemic illness: suspect septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy. Refer for same-day aspiration.
Unremitting night pain, weight loss or a history of cancer: arrange imaging to exclude tumour [r1].
After arthroscopy, calf pain, swelling or breathlessness: suspect DVT or PE, which occur after about 4 per 1000 procedures, and refer urgently [r15].

management.principles: Start with explanation, reassurance and supervised, progressive exercise therapy. Explain that meniscal tears are common, often painless findings with age [r2] and that surgery offers no extra benefit for most people [r4,r6,r7]. APM should not be the first line of treatment [r1], and the BMJ Rapid Recommendation makes a strong recommendation against arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease, including people with mechanical symptoms [r8]. ESSKA suggests that APM can be considered only after a standardised clinical and radiological evaluation and an unsatisfactory response to about 3 months of non-operative care [r1,r13]. Even then, placebo-controlled data show no added benefit in people with catching, locking or failed conservative care [r5,r16]. Address body weight, activity levels and coexisting osteoarthritis.

medical.name: Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy as first-line treatment
medical.description: No better than sham surgery at 12 and 24 months [r4,r16] and not superior to exercise therapy [r6,r7,r17]. Small, short-lived benefit at best, with harms including DVT, pulmonary embolism, infection and death [r15].

medical.name: APM after failed non-operative care
medical.description: ESSKA allows consideration after about 3 months of unsatisfactory non-operative care with persistent symptoms [r1,r13]. However, the BMJ guideline recommends against it [r8], and sham-controlled data show no extra benefit in those with mechanical symptoms or failed conservative care [r5,r16].

medical.name: Arthroscopic lavage and debridement
medical.description: Part of 'arthroscopy for degenerative knee'; no meaningful benefit and recognised harms [r15,r8].

medical.name: Simple analgesia and topical or oral NSAIDs
medical.description: Short courses to manage flares and allow exercise participation; consider comorbidities.

medical.name: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
medical.description: For a painful flare with effusion and synovitis, to settle inflammation and quadriceps inhibition so exercise can progress [r12].

physio.name: Supervised progressive exercise therapy
physio.description: 12 weeks of neuromuscular and strength training, 2–3 sessions per week, progressed by pain and effusion response. Equivalent to APM for function at 2 years, with better short-term thigh strength [r6,r7,r17,r18].

physio.name: Education and reassurance
physio.description: Explain that tears are common age-related findings, that pain is not a measure of damage, and that exercise is the evidence-based first step. Discuss the evidence on surgery honestly [r2,r3].

physio.name: Load and activity management
physio.description: Temporarily reduce deep loaded flexion, kneeling and prolonged stairs during flares while staying active; return gradually.

physio.name: Strategies for arthrogenic muscle inhibition
physio.description: Effusion control, cryotherapy, TENS or NMES to support quadriceps activation when inhibition limits training [r12].

physio.name: Weight management and general physical activity
physio.description: Support weight loss and aerobic activity in people who are overweight, as for knee osteoarthritis.

education: Meniscal tears are very common in people over 50, including many with no knee pain at all. The tear on your scan may not be the source of your pain.
Keyhole surgery to trim the meniscus works no better than a sham operation or a good exercise program for most people.
A 12-week exercise program improves pain and function and makes your thigh muscles stronger than surgery does.
Some pain during exercise is acceptable if it settles within 24 hours and swelling does not increase.
Clicking and catching are common and usually settle; true locking, where the knee cannot straighten, needs review.

rehab.overview: Exercise therapy follows the protocols used in the key trials: supervised neuromuscular and progressive strength training for about 12 weeks, with home exercise and education [r6,r7]. Progression is guided by pain (acceptable up to 5/10 during exercise if it settles within 24 hours) and effusion response, not by time. The aim is long-term self-management, so the final stage builds a sustainable routine.

stages.name: Settle & activate
goals: Restore quadriceps activation and comfortable range
precautions: Avoid deep loaded flexion and kneeling during a flare

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets
exercises.cues: Press the knee down and tighten the thigh

exercises.name: Stationary bike
exercises.cues: Seat high enough to avoid pain at the bottom of the stroke

stages.name: Neuromuscular control & strength
goals: Improve alignment and control in single-leg tasks
precautions: Pain up to 5/10 during exercise is acceptable if it settles within 24 hours

exercises.name: Step-up (progress height)
exercises.cues: Knee in line with the second toe; pelvis level

exercises.name: Single-leg balance with arm or trunk movements

progressionCriteria: No increase in effusion after sessions

stages.name: Progressive strength & function
goals: Tolerance of squatting, stairs and turning
Return to work and recreational activity
precautions: Introduce deep squatting and kneeling gradually; they load the posterior horn

exercises.name: Squat with load (progress depth)
exercises.cues: Sit back, keep weight through the heels

progressionCriteria: Quadriceps strength within 10–20% of the other side
Pain-free or minimal pain with daily tasks
Confidence with stairs, squatting and turning

stages.name: Self-management & activity
goals: Maintain gains and manage flares independently
precautions: A flare is not a re-injury: reduce load briefly, then rebuild

exercises.name: Balance and agility as needed for sport

progressionCriteria: KOOS or WOMET improvement reaches a level the patient finds acceptable

criteria: No or minimal effusion after training
Quadriceps strength close to the other side
Pain-free or acceptable pain with sport-specific movements such as squatting, turning and hopping
Confidence and an agreed plan for managing flares
tests: Hop tests in younger or athletic patients

prognosis: Most people improve over 3–12 months with exercise therapy. In trials, 19% of people allocated to exercise crossed over to surgery by 2 years without additional benefit [r6], 29% in the ESCAPE trial [r7], and 30% within 6 months in people with osteoarthritis [r17]. Outcomes after APM were no better than sham surgery at 24 months [r16]. Degenerative meniscal damage is part of the osteoarthritis process, so some people will progress over years; staying strong and active, and managing body weight, are the main modifiable factors [r3].
prevention: Maintain quadriceps and hip strength and healthy body weight through middle age.
Limit prolonged occupational kneeling and squatting where possible, or use knee protection and breaks [r9].
clinicalPearls: Treat the patient, not the scan. Over half of older adults with a meniscal tear on MRI have no knee symptoms [r2].
Catching and occasional locking do not predict benefit from APM; they were equally common after sham surgery [r5].
Order weight-bearing radiographs rather than MRI when imaging is needed for a middle-aged knee [r1].
Sudden, severe medial pain without trauma in an older adult is an insufficiency fracture until proven otherwise; do not simply label it a meniscal tear.
Use the trial protocols as your template: 12 weeks, 2–3 supervised sessions per week, progressive load [r6,r7].

animation.title: How a degenerative meniscal tear develops

captions.text: A 55-year-old kneels and squats in the garden, as they have for years.
Deep flexion loads the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.
Rising with a small twist is enough: no major injury is needed.
The ageing meniscus has lost capacity, so everyday load now exceeds it.
Pain builds gradually at the inner joint line, with on-and-off swelling.
Zooming into the right knee, viewed from the front with the patella reflected.

actions.text: Ageing meniscus: frayed and less resilient

captions.text: With age, the medial meniscus loses water and organised collagen, and frays.
Compression in flexion creates shear inside the wedge of the posterior horn.
A horizontal cleavage splits the meniscus into upper and lower leaves.
The damaged meniscus can bulge out of the joint and share less load.
The cartilage beside it is often wearing too: this is early osteoarthritis.
Synovitis and effusion drive pain flares, which is why exercise, not surgery, comes first.
Young meniscus: dense circumferential collagen bundles with healthy cells.
Repeated loading over decades, with fewer cells to maintain the matrix.
Shear splits the weakened bundles horizontally within the tissue.
Low blood supply and few cells mean no repair; symptoms settle as muscles and synovitis improve.
